title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: That same night, Rostov was on skirmish duty with a platoon, positioned ahead of Bagration's detachment. His hussars were stationed along the line in pairs, and he rode back and forth trying to fight off the drowsiness that kept overcoming him. Behind him stretched an enormous space where the army's campfires glowed dimly through the fog; ahead was nothing but misty darkness. Rostov strained to see into that foggy distance but could make out nothing: now something seemed to gleam gray, now something looked black, now tiny lights appeared to flicker where the enemy should be, then he thought it might just be his own eyes playing tricks. His eyelids kept drooping, and in his half-dreams he saw the Emperor, then Denisov, then memories of Moscow — and then he'd jerk his eyes open again to see the head and ears of his horse right in front of him, and sometimes, when he rode within six paces, the dark shapes of hussars nearby. But in the distance, the same misty darkness remained. "Why not?" thought Rostov. "It could easily happen. The Emperor might come across me and give me an order, just like he would any other officer. He'd say: 'Go find out what's out there.' There are plenty of stories about him noticing an officer by chance and taking him onto his personal staff. What if he gave me a place at his side? Oh, how I would protect him, how I would tell him the truth, how I would expose the people deceiving him!" And to make his devoted love for the sovereign feel more vivid, Rostov imagined an enemy or a treacherous German whom he would not only kill with pleasure but slap across the face right in front of the Emperor. Suddenly a distant shout jerked him awake. He started and opened his eyes.

"Where am I? Oh, right — the skirmish line. Password and countersign: shaft, Olmutz. What a shame our squadron's in reserve tomorrow," he thought. "I'll ask for leave to go to the front. This might be my only chance to see the Emperor. It won't be long until my duty's over. I'll make one more round, and when I get back I'll go to the general and ask." He adjusted himself in the saddle and urged his horse forward to ride another circuit past his hussars. It seemed to him that the sky was growing lighter. To the left he could see an illuminated slope, and facing it a dark hill that looked steep as a wall. On this hill there was a white patch that Rostov couldn't identify — was it a moonlit clearing in the woods, unmelted snow, or some white buildings? He even thought he saw something move on that white spot. "Probably snow... a spot... a patch — une tache," he thought. "Wait... it's not a patch... Natasha... my sister, those dark eyes... Na-tasha... (Won't she be amazed when I tell her I saw the Emperor?) Natasha... take my sabretache..." — "Keep to the right, your honor, there are bushes here," came the voice of a hussar he was riding past, already half asleep. Rostov lifted his head, which had drooped almost to his horse's mane, and pulled up beside the hussar. He was surrendering to an irresistible, youthful, childlike drowsiness. "But what was I thinking about? I mustn't forget. How am I going to speak to the Emperor? No, that's not it — that's tomorrow. Oh yes! Natasha... sabretache... saber them... Whom? The hussars... Ah, the hussars with their mustaches. Down Tverskaya Street rode the hussar with the mustache... I was thinking about him too, right across from Guryev's house... Old Guryev... Oh, but Denisov's a wonderful fellow. But that's all nonsense. The main thing is that the Emperor is here. The way he looked at me and wanted to say something but didn't dare... No, it was I who didn't dare. But that's all nonsense — the main thing is not to forget the important thought I was having. Yes, Na-tasha, sabretache, oh yes, yes! That's right!" And his head sank to his horse's neck once more. Suddenly he thought he was being shot at. "What? What? What?... Cut them down! What?" said Rostov, jolting awake. The moment he opened his eyes, he heard from ahead — from the enemy's direction — the long, drawn-out shouts of thousands of voices. His horse and the hussar's horse beside him pricked up their ears at the sound. Over where the shouting came from, a fire flared up and then went out, then another, and then all along the French line on the hill, fires blazed up one after another and the shouting grew louder and louder. Rostov could hear French words but couldn't make them out. The roar of so many voices was too great; all he could distinguish was "ahahah!" and "rrrr!"
"What's going on? What do you think that is?" said Rostov to the hussar beside him. "That must be the enemy's camp!"
The hussar didn't reply.
"Well? Don't you hear it?" Rostov asked again, after waiting for an answer.
"Who can say, your honor?" the hussar replied reluctantly.
"From the direction, it has to be the enemy," Rostov repeated.
"Maybe it is, maybe it's nothing," the hussar muttered. "It's dark... Steady!" he called to his restless horse.

Rostov's horse was getting agitated too, pawing at the frozen ground, pricking its ears at the noise, and staring toward the lights. The shouting grew even louder, merging into a roar that only an army of several thousand men could produce. The lights spread farther along what was probably the French camp's line. Rostov no longer felt sleepy. The jubilant, triumphant shouting from the enemy camp had an electrifying effect on him. "Long live the Emperor! The Emperor!" — he could now hear the words distinctly.
"They can't be far away — probably just beyond the stream," he said to the hussar beside him.

The hussar only sighed, said nothing, and coughed irritably. The sound of hooves approaching at a trot along the line of hussars reached them, and out of the foggy darkness the figure of a hussar sergeant appeared, looming as large as an elephant.
"Your honor, the generals!" said the sergeant, riding up to Rostov.

Rostov, still glancing back toward the fires and the shouting, rode with the sergeant to meet some mounted men coming along the line. One of them was on a white horse. It was Prince Bagration and Prince Dolgorukov, with their adjutants, who had come to see the strange spectacle of lights and shouts from the enemy camp for themselves. Rostov rode up to Bagration, made his report, and then joined the adjutants listening to the generals' conversation.
"Believe me," said Prince Dolgorukov, turning to Bagration, "it's nothing but a ruse. He's retreated and left fires and noise behind to fool us."

"I doubt it," said Bagration. "I saw them on that hill this evening. If they'd retreated, they would have pulled out from there too... Officer!" he said to Rostov. "Are the enemy's skirmishers still in position?"
"They were there this evening, but I can't say for certain now, your excellency. Shall I ride out with some of my hussars to check?" Rostov replied.
Bagration stopped and tried to make out Rostov's face through the mist before answering.
"Well, go and see," he said after a pause.
"Yes, sir."

Rostov spurred his horse, called Sergeant Fedchenko and two other hussars, told them to follow, and trotted downhill toward the source of the shouting. He felt both scared and excited to be riding alone with three hussars into that mysterious, dangerous, misty unknown where no one had gone before him. Bagration called after him from the hilltop not to cross the stream, but Rostov pretended not to hear and kept riding on, continually mistaking bushes for trees and ditches for men, and continually realizing his mistakes. After descending the hill at a trot, he could no longer see either the Russian or the French campfires, but he heard the French shouting more loudly and clearly. In the valley ahead he saw what looked like a river, but when he reached it, he found it was a road. Coming out onto the road, he reined in his horse, hesitating whether to follow it or cross it and ride up the black hillside. Staying on the road, which gleamed white through the mist, would have been safer — easier to spot people coming. "Follow me!" he said. He crossed the road and began galloping uphill toward where the French pickets had been posted that evening.

"Your honor, there he is!" cried one of the hussars behind him. And before Rostov could make out what the dark shape in the fog was, there was a flash, a report, and a bullet whizzed high overhead through the mist with a mournful whine and passed out of hearing. Another musket misfired but flashed in the pan. Rostov wheeled his horse around and galloped back. Four more shots rang out at intervals, the bullets whistling past somewhere in the fog, each with a different pitch. Rostov eased his horse to a walk — the animal's spirits had risen with the firing, just like his own — and headed back at a leisurely pace. "More! Come on, more!" a happy voice said inside him. But no more shots came.
Only when he was close to Bagration did Rostov let his horse gallop again, and he rode up to the general with his hand at the salute.
Dolgorukov was still insisting that the French had retreated and had only left fires behind to trick them.
"What does that prove?" he was saying as Rostov rode up. "They could retreat and leave the pickets."
"It's clear they haven't all gone, Prince," said Bagration. "Let's wait until tomorrow morning — we'll find out everything then."

"The picket is still on the hill, your excellency — right where it was this evening," Rostov reported, leaning forward with his hand at the salute, unable to suppress the smile of exhilaration that his ride and especially the sound of the bullets had produced.
"Very good, very good," said Bagration. "Thank you, officer."
"Your excellency," said Rostov, "may I ask a favor?"
"What is it?"
"Our squadron is supposed to be in reserve tomorrow. May I request to be attached to the first squadron?"
"What's your name?"
"Count Rostov."
"Oh, very well — you may remain in my personal retinue."
"Count Ilya Rostov's son?" asked Dolgorukov.
But Rostov didn't reply.
"Then I can count on it, your excellency?"
"I'll give the order."
"Tomorrow I might even be sent with a message to the Emperor," Rostov thought.
"Thank God!"

The fires and shouting in the enemy camp were caused by the fact that Napoleon's proclamation was being read to the troops, and the Emperor himself was riding through his bivouacs. The soldiers, catching sight of him, lit bundles of straw and ran after him shouting, "Long live the Emperor!" Napoleon's proclamation read as follows:

Soldiers! The Russian army is advancing against you to avenge the Austrian army of Ulm. These are the same battalions you crushed at Hollabrunn and have been chasing ever since. The position we hold is a strong one, and while they march to outflank me on the right, they will expose their flank. Soldiers! I will personally direct your battalions. I will stay out of the firing line if, with your customary bravery, you carry chaos and confusion into the enemy's ranks. But should victory be in doubt even for a moment, you will see your Emperor expose himself to the enemy's first blows, for there must be no uncertainty about victory — especially on this day, when the honor of the French infantry is at stake, so vital to the honor of our nation.

Do not break ranks on the excuse of helping the wounded! Let every man be filled with the conviction that we must defeat these mercenaries of England, who harbor such hatred for our nation! This victory will end our campaign, and we can return to winter quarters where fresh French troops being raised in France will join us. The peace I will then make will be worthy of my people, of you, and of myself.
NAPOLEON
